prompt: ok so I need some help. I sell shift scheduling software (Rostrly, about 38k/yr for this size of customer). Demo was 3 weeks ago with Priya Nandakumar, ops lead at Westmoor Health, a group of 4 regional hospitals. She loved it, said on the call 'this would save my coordinators a day a week'. But she also mentioned finance, IT and the head of nursing all have to sign before anything happens. I sent the recap + pricing the next day. Followed up twice by email since. Nothing. Not a no, just silence. My manager says 'just keep chasing Priya'. What do I actually do now?
rubric: Identifies that the deal likely stalled because finance, IT and the head of nursing have not been engaged or given a reason to say yes, rather than treating it only as a follow-up cadence problem.

Recommends a concrete next move through Priya (for example asking her directly where it stands and what each of the three signers will need, or offering material or a short session aimed at a specific signer) instead of just sending more chase emails.
Suggests at least one specific question or message the rep can actually send or say, worded in plain language.
Gives a way to tell whether the deal is real or dead (for example a clear ask with a date, or accepting a no) rather than chasing indefinitely.
Does not invent facts about Westmoor Health such as budget cycles, named people beyond those given, or what the nursing head or IT objected to.

prompt: Plan a one-hour call for me Thursday with Halvorsen Freight (3PL, 5 warehouses in the midwest). We sell warehouse labour planning software. Attendees: Dana Whitfield (finance director), Marco Ruiz (warehouse manager, Joliet site), two shift leads I've never met, Kevin from IT, and Ola from procurement. Problem is they don't agree on what the problem is. Marco thinks it's overtime, Dana keeps talking about forecasting accuracy, and the shift leads apparently think scheduling is fine and the real issue is people not showing up. I've only talked to Marco and Dana one-on-one. Give me the agenda and what I should actually say.
rubric: Puts agreeing on the problem (or problems) before any product demo or pitch, and gives the group a way to surface and compare the different views of Marco, Dana and the shift leads.
Gives the shift leads, IT and procurement a defined moment or question in the hour, rather than letting the two people the rep already knows dominate.
Includes a time-boxed agenda that adds up to about an hour and contains at least some actual wording the rep can use (an opening, key questions, or a closing ask).
Ends the call with a specific next step to be agreed in the room (who does what by when), not a vague 'we'll follow up'.
Does not invent numbers about Halvorsen's overtime, absence rates or forecast error, or claim product results the prompt does not give.

prompt: Deal: 210k ARR data platform, Kintaro Retail. Their security team has been 'reviewing' us for six weeks. Our sponsor Elena Brandt (VP marketing) says they're just slow and not to worry. My AE says Elena is our champion because she takes every call and tells us what's going on internally. The AE now wants to spend the next two weeks building a full custom proposal. Do we (a) build the proposal, (b) push on the security review first, or (c) something else? And how do I tell if Elena is actually a champion or just friendly?
rubric: Makes a clear choice among the options (or a clearly stated alternative) and gives the reason tied to the six-week security stall, instead of listing pros and cons without deciding.

Distinguishes a person who shares information from one who will act for the deal, and gives at least one concrete test of Elena (for example asking her to arrange a direct conversation with the security lead, or to share what security has actually asked for and by when).
Recommends finding out what the security review is actually waiting on, ideally by direct contact with the security team, rather than accepting 'they're just slow'.
Advises against committing two weeks of proposal work until the stall and Elena's role are tested, or explains clearly why proceeding anyway is justified.
Does not invent details about Kintaro's security process, questionnaires, or internal politics that the prompt does not provide.

prompt: Need a postmortem on this one. We sell fleet telematics. Prospect was Brightline Transit (bus operator, ~600 vehicles). I did one-to-ones with the ops director, the maintenance manager, the CFO and the head of IT over about a month. Every single one of them said yes, they love it, makes sense. So we sent a joint proposal for all 600 vehicles, around 290k over 3 years. It came back approved for 200 vehicles only, 'as a pilot'. Nobody warned me. What happened, and what should I do differently next time? Also is there anything to do with this deal now or do I just take the 200?
rubric: Offers a plausible explanation that individual yeses in one-to-ones did not equal a group decision (for example the four never discussed priorities, budget or risk together, or someone's concern only surfaced when they met), and is honest that it is a likely reading, not a certainty.

Names at least one specific thing to do differently next time, such as getting the group together to agree the problem and criteria before the proposal, or testing what each person would actually sign off on.
Gives practical advice on the current deal (for example accepting the 200 while agreeing in writing what the pilot must show for expansion, by when, and who decides).
Suggests asking Brightline directly why it was cut rather than only guessing.
Does not make up what any Brightline person said or thought beyond what the prompt states.

prompt:
I messed up. In yesterday's demo with Ostrander Bank their IT lead (Tomasz) asked if we support SCIM provisioning with Okta groups. I said 'yes, I believe so'. We don't. We support SAML SSO with Okta but user provisioning is manual or CSV, and SCIM isn't on a committed roadmap. Here's the email I drafted, can you fix it?

"Hi Tomasz, great demo yesterday! Quick note on SCIM: our identity story is evolving rapidly and we have flexible options that many of our enterprise customers find works great alongside Okta. Happy to dig in more on a call!"

Also, this keeps happening to me on discovery calls, engineers ask technical stuff I can't answer on the spot. Give me a few lines I can use that don't make me look clueless.
rubric: The rewritten email states plainly that the earlier answer was wrong and that SCIM provisioning is not supported, and says what is supported (SAML SSO with Okta; manual or CSV provisioning), without spin like 'evolving rapidly' or 'flexible options'.
The email does not suggest SCIM is coming or on the roadmap, and does not invent workarounds, customer examples or dates not given in the prompt.
The email is short and offers a useful next step (for example a call with a technical colleague to see whether CSV provisioning fits their setup).
The lines for future calls are honest ways to say 'I don't know' that commit to a specific follow-up (who will answer and roughly when), with no bluffing or vague deflection.
Advises sending the correction promptly rather than waiting for Tomasz to find out.

prompt: We're presenting our proposal to Calderon Foods' buying committee of five on Thursday (contract mgmt software, ~85k/yr, replacing their current vendor DocuVault). Committee is legal counsel, the CFO, two regional ops managers and Rachel Okafor from procurement. Rachel has said in two emails that she'd rather just renew with DocuVault, mainly because switching is a hassle and DocuVault's been 'fine'. The ops managers are the ones who pushed for a change. How do I run the meeting with her in the room?
rubric: Recommends a step before Thursday, such as a direct conversation with Rachel to understand her concerns about switching, rather than leaving her view to come up for the first time in the meeting.
In the meeting plan, Rachel's preference for renewing is stated fairly and her switching concerns (effort, risk) are addressed openly, not dismissed or argued away.
Proposes getting the whole committee to agree the decision criteria (or what 'fine' is costing them) before or while comparing options.
Avoids tactics that corner or embarrass Rachel in front of colleagues or try to go around her.
Does not invent DocuVault weaknesses, migration timelines or Calderon pain points the prompt does not state; where such facts would help, it says to find them out.

prompt: prep my 20 min discovery call tomorrow with Ines Varga, she runs a one-person design studio (brand work for small businesses). we sell an invoicing + time tracking tool, 19/month. she found us through a newsletter and booked the call herself. she decides alone, no partners, no accountant involved in the purchase.
rubric: The plan treats Ines as the sole decision maker and does not add stakeholder mapping, champion-building, buying-committee or procurement steps.
The plan fits 20 minutes and is proportionate to a 19/month purchase, with a short set of focused questions about how she invoices and tracks time today and what is annoying her.
Includes a simple, concrete close for the call (for example starting a trial during or right after the call, or setting a clear next step) suited to a single buyer.
Does not invent facts about Ines's studio, her current tools, or her problems.
Is short; it does not pad with long frameworks or a lengthy theory section.

prompt: prospect asked 'can you export to CSV?' on the call earlier, we can (any report, one click, top right). they're probably going to ask again on the follow-up. what's the best way to answer?
rubric: Recommends a direct yes, ideally with a quick show or one-line description of where the export is, and then stopping.
Does not prescribe elaborate questioning rituals, discovery frameworks or objection-handling steps for a simple yes question; at most one light optional question about what they need the export for.
Does not invent capabilities beyond what the prompt states (for example scheduled exports, API access or other formats).
The whole answer is brief, a few lines rather than a long guide.

prompt: Small one. Gus Ferreira owns Ferreira Plumbing (11 vans). Had a 30 min demo of our dispatch app yesterday, at the end he said 'this is what I need, send me the order form, we'll start the 1st'. It's 4,200/yr. He's the owner and signs everything himself. My new sales manager wants me to hold off and first run a mutual action plan, loop in his office manager and the two senior techs, and do a business case doc. Should I do that or just send the form?
rubric: Recommends sending the order form now (or clearly says the extra process is not needed), giving the reason that the owner is the sole signer and has asked to buy.
Limits any extra steps to light, practical ones that help the start on the 1st (for example confirming billing details or onboarding the office manager after signing), not as gates before the sale.
Does not invent risks, objections or other decision makers that the prompt does not suggest.
Gives a brief way to answer the sales manager respectfully.
Is short and to the point.
